title: Disorders of the Pleural Cavity and Lung Expansion
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers what happens when the pleural space fills with lymph, blood, fluid, pus, or air, when a lung segment collapses, and when the mediastinum or chest wall is injured. The unifying idea is that the lung stays expanded only because a thin, sealed pleural space holds subatmospheric pressure between an inward-recoiling lung and an outward-springing chest wall. Board questions give a pleural fluid analysis, a tracheal position, a percussion note, or a trauma scenario and ask you to name the process. If you can explain what each substance does to pleural pressure and lung volume, and which way it moves the mediastinum, you can reason through most of these items.
prerequisites: Anatomy of the pleurae, mediastinum, thoracic duct, and diaphragm (PU-4)
Lung and chest wall recoil, intrapleural pressure, and compliance (PU-6)
Starling forces across capillaries and lymphatic drainage
Shunt, V/Q mismatch, and the alveolar gas equation (PU-7)
Acute inflammation, neutrophil exudates, and organization by fibrosis

connections.how: Pneumothorax and flail chest are direct demonstrations of the opposing recoil of lung and chest wall that sets intrapleural pressure.
Asbestosis is the interstitial counterpart of asbestos pleural disease, and fibrothorax and diffuse pleural thickening produce extraparenchymal restriction.
Pneumonia organisms cause parapneumonic effusion and empyema, and Bacillus anthracis spores cause hemorrhagic mediastinitis.
Heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome produce transudates by changing hydrostatic or oncotic pressure, and tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock.
Lymphoma causes chylothorax, malignancy causes exudates and hemothorax, and asbestos drives bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma.

terms.def: The pressure in the thin pleural space, about -5 cm H2O at functional residual capacity, created by the lung recoiling inward and the chest wall springing outward.
Low-protein pleural fluid formed when hydrostatic or oncotic pressure changes push fluid across intact capillaries and pleura.
Protein-rich pleural fluid formed when inflamed, infected, or invaded pleura or lymphatic obstruction lets protein, cells, and LDH accumulate.
Milky intestinal lymph rich in chylomicrons, triglycerides, and lymphocytes, carried to the venous system by the thoracic duct.
A thick fibrous peel over the pleura, formed by organization of retained blood or pus, that encases and restricts the lung.
Incomplete expansion or collapse of previously aerated lung, classified as resorption, compression, or contraction.
Pneumothorax in which a one-way valve traps air so pleural pressure becomes positive, shifting the mediastinum and impairing venous return.
An asbestos fiber or other inhaled fiber coated by macrophages with iron-containing protein, seen as a golden brown beaded rod that stains with Prussian blue.
Three comparisons of pleural fluid with serum protein and LDH; meeting any one classifies the fluid as an exudate.
A crunching or clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, heard over the precordium in pneumomediastinum.
Inward movement of a flail chest wall segment during inspiration and outward movement during expiration, opposite to the rest of the chest.

sections.title: Chylothorax: thoracic duct disruption and milky pleural fluid

blocks.text: Intestinal lacteals absorb dietary long-chain fatty acids packaged as chylomicrons, and this lymph (chyle) drains into the cisterna chyli near the upper lumbar vertebrae. The thoracic duct carries it upward through the aortic hiatus at about T12, ascends in the posterior mediastinum to the right of the midline between the aorta and the azygos vein, crosses to the left at about T4 to T6, and empties at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. It returns about 1.5 to 2.5 L of chyle per day, more after a fatty meal.

blocks.title: Path of chyle and the side of a chylothorax
steps: Lacteals load chylomicrons into intestinal lymph
Cisterna chyli collects lymph near the upper lumbar spine
Duct enters thorax through aortic hiatus at T12
Ascends right of midline between aorta and azygos
Crosses left at about T4 to T6
Drains at left subclavian and internal jugular junction
blocks.caption: Injury below the crossing usually produces a right chylothorax; injury above it usually produces a left one.

blocks.text: Chylothorax is chyle in the pleural space after the duct or its tributaries are torn or blocked. Traumatic causes include penetrating and blunt chest injury and, most often, thoracic surgery (esophagectomy, cardiac and aortic surgery) along the duct's course. Nontraumatic causes are dominated by malignancy, and lymphoma is the leading malignant cause because enlarged mediastinal nodes compress or invade the duct and raise pressure in the lymphatics behind the block. Less common causes include lymphangioleiomyomatosis, congenital lymphatic malformations, and central venous thrombosis that raises pressure at the duct's outlet.

The fluid looks milky because suspended chylomicrons scatter light. Its defining laboratory finding is a pleural triglyceride concentration above 110 mg/dL, and chylomicrons on lipoprotein analysis confirm it. A triglyceride level below 50 mg/dL makes chylothorax unlikely, and values between need lipoprotein testing. The fluid stays milky after centrifugation (cells in empyema settle and leave a clear supernatant), is lymphocyte predominant because chyle carries lymphocytes, and is usually odorless. A fasting patient may produce clear chyle, so a nonmilky fluid does not exclude the diagnosis.

blocks.title: Telling chylothorax from look-alike milky fluids
rows: Chyle leaks from injured or blocked thoracic duct
Cholesterol accumulates in a long-standing effusion with thick pleura (tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis)
Bacterial infection with neutrophils in the pleural space
blocks.caption: Triglycerides and chylomicrons identify chyle; cholesterol crystals identify a pseudochylothorax; settling cells identify pus.

blocks.text: Because chyle carries fat, protein, fat-soluble vitamins, and lymphocytes, a persistent leak drains all of them. Prolonged chylothorax therefore produces malnutrition, hypoalbuminemia, lymphopenia, and impaired cell-mediated immunity, in addition to the restrictive effects of a large effusion. Chyle is relatively bacteriostatic, so infection of the collection itself is uncommon.

sections.title: Hemothorax: bleeding into the pleural space and its consequences

blocks.text: Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space. Bloody-looking fluid needs only a small amount of blood (a red blood cell count of about 5,000 to 10,000 per microliter already looks pink), so hemothorax is defined by a pleural fluid hematocrit at least half (50%) of the patient's blood hematocrit. A serosanguineous malignant effusion usually has a fluid hematocrit far below that level.

Trauma is the most common cause. Penetrating wounds and rib fractures tear intercostal vessels and the internal thoracic artery, which carry systemic arterial pressure, and these bleed far more briskly than lung parenchyma, which is supplied by the low-pressure pulmonary circulation. Nontraumatic causes include rupture of an aortic dissection or aneurysm (typically into the left pleural space), pleural or metastatic malignancy, mesothelioma, ruptured pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, catamenial hemothorax from thoracic endometriosis, coagulopathy or anticoagulation, and iatrogenic injury from procedures.

Each hemithorax can hold a large share of the circulating volume, often stated as 30% to 40%, so bleeding can be concealed there. A large hemothorax causes two problems at once. First, loss of intravascular volume lowers preload and produces hypovolemic shock: tachycardia, hypotension, cool skin, and flat neck veins. Second, the space-occupying blood compresses the lung, causing compression atelectasis, shunt, and hypoxemia, and a very large collection pushes the mediastinum toward the opposite side. Examination shows dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds and fremitus on the affected side.

blocks.title: From hemothorax to fibrothorax
steps: Torn vessel bleeds into the pleural space
Volume loss lowers preload and causes hypovolemic shock
Collection compresses lung, causing atelectasis and hypoxemia
Movement partly defibrinates blood, but retained clot persists
Fibroblasts organize clot into a fibrous pleural peel
Peel traps the lung: fibrothorax with restriction
blocks.caption: Early danger is volume loss; late danger is organization of retained clot into a restrictive peel.

blocks.text: Over days, blood that is not evacuated begins to organize. Motion of the heart, lungs, and diaphragm partly defibrinates pleural blood, which is why some of it stays liquid, but retained clot is invaded by fibroblasts and capillaries, as in organization anywhere. The result is fibrothorax, a thick collagenous peel over the visceral and parietal pleura that prevents the lung from expanding. It produces a restrictive pattern with reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity and a small, immobile hemithorax with rib crowding. Retained clot is also a good culture medium, so secondary empyema is another late complication.

blocks.predict: A trauma patient has hypotension and absent breath sounds on the left. Percussion is dull and the neck veins are flat. Is this a hemothorax or a tension pneumothorax?
blocks.explain: Dullness and flat neck veins point to hemothorax with hypovolemia. Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and distended neck veins because venous return is obstructed, not because volume is lost.
blocks.check: Compare the shock mechanism here with the tension pneumothorax discussion in C05.

blocks.text: Atelectasis is incomplete expansion or collapse of previously aerated lung. It is classified by mechanism as resorption (obstructive), compression, or contraction (cicatrization). The first two are reversible once the cause is removed, and the direction of mediastinal shift distinguishes them.

Resorption atelectasis follows complete obstruction of an airway by a mucus plug (postoperative patients, asthma, bronchiectasis), an endobronchial tumor, or an aspirated foreign body. Gas in the trapped alveoli is still exposed to perfusing capillaries, and mixed venous blood has a total gas pressure below atmospheric. Venous PO2 is about 40 mmHg, far below the alveolar value of about 100 mmHg, while venous PCO2 is only about 6 mmHg higher than alveolar PCO2, so the sum of venous gas pressures is about 700 mmHg against an alveolar sum of 760 mmHg. Oxygen leaves the alveolus first, then nitrogen slowly follows down its own gradient, and the segment shrinks until it is airless. When the trapped gas is pure oxygen, as during breathing of 100% oxygen, there is no nitrogen to slow the process and collapse occurs within minutes.

blocks.title: Mechanism of resorption atelectasis
steps: Plug, tumor, or foreign body completely blocks a bronchus
Distal alveolar gas can no longer be replenished
Capillary blood absorbs oxygen, then nitrogen, from trapped gas
Alveoli collapse and the lobe loses volume
Lost volume pulls trachea and mediastinum toward the collapse
blocks.caption: Subatmospheric total gas pressure in venous blood drives absorption of trapped alveolar gas.

blocks.text: Because the collapsed lobe occupies less space, the hemithorax loses volume: the trachea and mediastinum move toward the collapse, the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm rises, and the rib spaces narrow. Compression atelectasis is the opposite situation. Fluid (effusion, hemothorax), air (pneumothorax), or a mass fills the pleural space, the lung is passively squeezed, and a large collection pushes the mediastinum away from the lesion. Contraction atelectasis occurs when local or generalized fibrosis prevents full expansion; like resorption it pulls structures toward the lesion, but it is not reversible.

blocks.title: Types of atelectasis
rows: Complete airway obstruction: mucus plug, tumor, foreign body
Pleural fluid, air, or mass pressing on lung
Yes, if the collection is removed
blocks.caption: Volume loss pulls structures toward the lesion; added volume in the pleural space pushes them away.

blocks.text: Collapsed alveoli remain perfused, so atelectasis creates intrapulmonary shunt. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some blood away and limits the fall in PaO2, and the hypoxemia responds poorly to supplemental oxygen because shunted blood never meets alveolar gas. Over the collapsed region, percussion is dull and breath sounds and fremitus are reduced when the bronchus is occluded. Collapsed lung beyond an obstruction clears secretions poorly and is prone to infection, which is why a persistent lobar collapse in an adult smoker raises concern for an obstructing carcinoma.

blocks.predict: A dense opacity fills the left hemithorax. In patient A the trachea is pulled to the left; in patient B it is pushed to the right. What process explains each?
blocks.explain: Patient A has lost volume, as in complete left lung collapse from an obstructed main bronchus. Patient B has added volume in the pleural space, as in a massive effusion that pushes the mediastinum away.
blocks.check: Compare with the atelectasis types table and the effusion findings in C06.

sections.title: Asbestos-related pleural disease and cancer risk

blocks.text: Asbestos is a group of fibrous silicates. Serpentine chrysotile fibers are curly and flexible and tend to impact in larger airways, where mucociliary clearance and dissolution remove many of them. Amphibole fibers (crocidolite, amosite) are straight, stiff, and thin, so they penetrate deep into the lung, cross into the interstitium, and migrate to the pleura. Amphiboles are more pathogenic, especially for mesothelioma. Fibers too long for a macrophage to engulf cause frustrated phagocytosis: the macrophage keeps producing reactive oxygen species and releases cytokines and growth factors (including TGF-beta and PDGF) that recruit fibroblasts and damage DNA.

Pleural plaques are the most common lesion of asbestos exposure. They are well-circumscribed plates of dense, hyalinized collagen on the parietal pleura, typically over the posterolateral chest wall and the domes of the diaphragm, and they often calcify. They rarely contain asbestos bodies, usually cause no symptoms, and mark exposure rather than disease; they do not become mesothelioma. Benign asbestos pleural effusion is an exudate, often bloody, that can appear within one to two decades of exposure, earlier than other asbestos lesions. Diffuse pleural fibrosis involves the visceral pleura, often follows recurrent effusion, blunts the costophrenic angle, and can restrict ventilation; folding of thickened pleura into the lung produces rounded atelectasis. Asbestosis itself, interstitial fibrosis that begins in the lower lobes, is covered in PU-14-A.

Asbestos bodies, a type of ferruginous body, form when macrophages coat a fiber with iron-containing protein (ferritin and hemosiderin). In tissue they are golden brown, fusiform or beaded rods with a thin translucent core, and they stain blue with Prussian blue. They prove exposure, but small numbers occur in many urban adults without disease, so the diagnosis of asbestosis requires fibrosis as well.

blocks.title: Asbestos lesions of the pleura and lung
rows: Parietal pleura, posterolateral wall and diaphragm; often calcified
Most common lesion; marker of exposure; benign
Most frequent asbestos-related cancer; risk multiplied by smoking
Diffuse pleural tumor encasing the lung
Long latency; risk not increased by smoking
blocks.caption: Plaques signal exposure; carcinoma and mesothelioma are the lethal outcomes.

blocks.text: Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most frequent malignancy in asbestos-exposed people. Asbestos alone raises the risk about fivefold, and the combination with smoking is multiplicative rather than additive, with risk often quoted as about 50 times that of unexposed nonsmokers. One proposed reason is that fibers adsorb and concentrate carcinogens from smoke and deliver them to epithelial cells while sustaining oxidant injury. Malignant mesothelioma, by contrast, is strongly linked to asbestos (especially amphiboles) with a latency of roughly 25 to 40 years or more and smoking does not raise its risk. Mesothelioma encases the lung in a thick rind and typically produces a hemorrhagic effusion; its pathology is taught in PU-14-F.

The lung recoils inward and the chest wall springs outward, and the sealed pleural space between them holds a pressure of about -5 cm H2O at functional residual capacity. If air enters the space from a ruptured alveolus or through the chest wall, pleural pressure rises toward atmospheric, the lung collapses toward the hilum under its own elastic recoil, and the chest wall on that side springs slightly outward. Air between lung and chest wall percusses as hyperresonant and blocks transmission of breath sounds and vocal vibration, so the classic findings are hyperresonance, reduced or absent breath sounds, and reduced tactile fremitus on the affected side.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without known lung disease, typically in tall, thin young men, and smoking increases the risk substantially. It results from rupture of small subpleural blebs at the lung apex. Pleural pressure is more negative at the apex than at the base because of gravity and the weight of the lung, so apical alveoli are more distended, and this stress is greater in a tall chest. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax complicates underlying lung disease: COPD (ruptured emphysematous bullae, the most common cause), cystic fibrosis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and necrotizing infections. Because reserve is already reduced, a secondary pneumothorax causes more hypoxemia for its size. Traumatic and iatrogenic pneumothorax (central line placement, lung biopsy, mechanical ventilation) form a third group.

blocks.title: The one-way valve in tension pneumothorax
steps: Inspiration opens a flap and draws air into the pleural space
Expiration closes the flap and traps the air
Pleural pressure becomes positive and rises with each breath
Lung collapses and mediastinum shifts to the opposite side
Venae cavae kink and compress; venous return falls
Hypoxemia drives harder breathing, pulling in more air
blocks.caption: Each breath adds air that cannot leave, so pressure climbs until cardiac output fails.

blocks.text: Tension pneumothorax develops when a tissue flap acts as a one-way valve. Positive and rising intrapleural pressure collapses the ipsilateral lung completely, pushes the trachea and mediastinum toward the opposite side, compresses the contralateral lung, and impairs filling of the right heart by compressing and kinking the venae cavae and raising intrathoracic pressure. The result is obstructive shock: tachycardia, hypotension, and distended neck veins (blood backs up because it cannot enter the chest), with severe hypoxemia. Positive pressure ventilation and trauma make tension physiology more likely because air is forced into the space with each breath.

blocks.title: Comparing the three main forms of pneumothorax
rows: Tall, thin young man, often a smoker
Older patient with COPD, cystic fibrosis, or other lung disease
Trauma or positive pressure ventilation; any pneumothorax can progress
Rupture of bulla or diseased lung
One-way valve traps air under positive pressure
Deviated away from the affected side
Usually stable, but hypoxemia more severe
blocks.caption: Tracheal deviation and hemodynamic collapse distinguish tension from simple pneumothorax.

sections.title: Pleural effusion: Starling forces and Light criteria

blocks.text: Normally each pleural space contains only about 0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg of fluid. It filters mainly from systemic capillaries of the parietal pleura, under Starling forces, and leaves through stomata and lymphatics of the parietal pleura, which can increase their drainage many times when filtration rises. An effusion forms when filtration exceeds lymphatic capacity, either because pressures change across an intact membrane or because the membrane or its lymphatics are damaged.

A transudate forms when hydrostatic pressure rises or oncotic pressure falls while the capillaries and pleura are intact, so protein, cells, and LDH are largely held back. Heart failure is the most common cause of any pleural effusion: raised pulmonary venous pressure drives interstitial edema that crosses the visceral pleura, and the effusions are usually bilateral or right-sided. Cirrhosis causes hepatic hydrothorax, typically on the right, as ascites passes through small diaphragmatic defects under the negative pleural pressure. Nephrotic syndrome lowers plasma oncotic pressure through urinary albumin loss. An exudate forms when inflammation, infection, or tumor makes the pleural capillaries leaky or blocks lymphatic drainage, so protein and LDH (released from inflammatory and tumor cells) accumulate.

blocks.title: Light criteria (exudate if any one is met)
rows: A leaky membrane lets plasma protein into the fluid
Inflammatory and tumor cells release LDH locally
Above two thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH
Absolute marker of local cell injury and turnover
blocks.caption: A transudate meets none of the three; the criteria are very sensitive for exudates but can misclassify some transudates.

blocks.title: Common causes by category
rows: Parapneumonic effusion and empyema (most common exudate)
Malignancy: lung and breast carcinoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma
Rheumatoid arthritis and SLE; chylothorax and hemothorax
blocks.caption: Pressure problems produce transudates; pleural disease produces exudates.

blocks.text: Light criteria identify nearly all exudates, but about one quarter of transudates are misclassified as exudates, most often in heart failure after diuresis concentrates protein and LDH in the remaining fluid. A serum minus pleural albumin gradient above 1.2 g/dL supports a transudate in that setting. Over any large effusion, percussion is stony dull, fremitus and breath sounds are reduced, egophony may be heard at the upper border where lung is compressed, and a massive effusion pushes the mediastinum away. On an upright posteroanterior radiograph about 200 mL is needed to blunt the costophrenic angle, and a lateral view shows smaller volumes.

blocks.title: Applying Light criteria
blocks.text: Pleural protein is 3.0 g/dL with serum protein 7.0 g/dL; pleural LDH is 110 U/L with serum LDH 200 U/L and a serum upper limit of 220 U/L. Protein ratio: 3.0 / 7.0 = 0.43, below 0.5, so not exudative. LDH ratio: 110 / 200 = 0.55, below 0.6, so not exudative. Two thirds of 220 is about 147 U/L, and 110 is below it, so not exudative. No criterion is met, so the fluid is a transudate, consistent with heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome. If pleural LDH had been 160 U/L, the third criterion alone would make it an exudate, because meeting any single criterion is enough.

Empyema is pus in the pleural space, most often a progression of a parapneumonic effusion. Bacteria from adjacent pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, the Streptococcus anginosus group, and oral anaerobes after aspiration) invade the effusion, and neutrophils follow. Both neutrophils and bacteria metabolize glucose anaerobically to lactate and produce CO2, so the fluid becomes acidic (pH below about 7.2) with low glucose (below about 60 mg/dL) and very high LDH from cell lysis. Untreated, the process moves from a free-flowing exudate to fibrin deposition and loculation, then to organization into a fibrous peel that traps the lung, the same end point as a retained hemothorax. Patients have persistent fever and pleuritic pain after an apparently resolving pneumonia.

blocks.title: Evolution of a parapneumonic effusion to empyema
steps: Pneumonia inflames the visceral pleura
Leaky capillaries produce a sterile free-flowing exudate
Bacteria invade and neutrophils pour in
Glycolysis lowers pleural glucose and pH
Fibrin forms loculations and frank pus
Fibroblasts lay down a restrictive pleural peel
blocks.caption: Low pH, low glucose, and high LDH reflect intense local metabolism by neutrophils and bacteria.

blocks.text: The mediastinum is a continuous connective tissue compartment, so infection or air that enters it spreads widely. Acute mediastinitis has three classic sources. Esophageal perforation, most often iatrogenic during endoscopy and also from forceful vomiting (Boerhaave syndrome, usually a tear of the distal left posterolateral wall), releases oral flora and gastric contents. Deep sternal wound infection follows median sternotomy. Descending infection from odontogenic or retropharyngeal abscesses travels down the cervical fascial planes. Inhalational anthrax is a special case: alveolar macrophages carry Bacillus anthracis spores to mediastinal lymph nodes, where they germinate and release edema toxin and lethal toxin, producing hemorrhagic necrotizing lymphadenitis and mediastinitis with a widened mediastinum and hemorrhagic pleural effusions, often without a true pneumonia.

Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinum. Most cases begin with alveolar rupture during high intrathoracic pressure (asthma, forceful Valsalva, vomiting, inhaled drug use). Air tracks along the bronchovascular sheaths to the hilum and into the mediastinum (the Macklin effect), then continues into the neck and chest wall, producing subcutaneous emphysema that crackles under the fingers (crepitus). The Hamman sign is a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat as the heart moves against air-filled tissue. Esophageal or tracheobronchial rupture causes a more dangerous pneumomediastinum because it is often accompanied by mediastinitis.

Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costosternal junctions, usually involving several of the second to fifth ribs, without visible swelling (Tietze syndrome is the variant with localized swelling, usually at a single upper junction). The pain arises from the chest wall itself, so pressing on the affected junction reproduces it exactly. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion, because reproducible tenderness does not by itself exclude cardiac or pulmonary causes of chest pain.

blocks.title: Distinguishing features
rows: Pus; low pH and glucose; high LDH; organisms on Gram stain
Pain reproduced by pressing the costal cartilages
blocks.caption: Each condition is identified by its setting plus one characteristic finding.

sections.title: Chest trauma: flail chest, contusion, open pneumothorax, and diaphragmatic rupture

blocks.text: Flail chest occurs when several adjacent ribs (commonly defined as three or more) are each fractured in two or more places, leaving a segment of chest wall that is no longer attached to the rest of the cage. The segment follows pleural pressure instead of the chest wall: it is sucked inward during inspiration as pleural pressure falls and bulges outward during expiration. This paradoxical motion reduces effective tidal volume, and pain causes splinting that promotes atelectasis. The force needed to create a flail segment almost always bruises the lung beneath, and that contusion is usually the main cause of hypoxemia.

Pulmonary contusion is hemorrhage and edema in the alveoli and interstitium from direct impact. Blood and edema fluid flood alveoli that remain perfused, creating intrapulmonary shunt and reduced compliance. Because edema and inflammation continue to accumulate, hypoxemia and radiographic opacities typically worsen over the first 24 to 48 hours, and the initial radiograph can underestimate the injury. Opacities are patchy and do not respect lobar boundaries, unlike lobar pneumonia, and they usually resolve within about a week unless pneumonia or ARDS supervenes.

Open pneumothorax results from a chest wall defect that communicates with the pleural space. When the opening is larger than about two thirds of the tracheal diameter, it offers less resistance than the airway, so air moves preferentially through the wound with each inspiration (a sucking chest wound). The ipsilateral lung collapses and ventilation falls sharply. If tissue around the wound forms a flap valve, the open pneumothorax can convert to tension physiology.

Blunt diaphragmatic rupture is diagnosed more often on the left because the liver buffers the right hemidiaphragm. A sudden rise in abdominal pressure tears the muscle, and the abdomen-to-chest pressure gradient draws stomach, colon, or spleen into the left hemithorax, giving bowel sounds in the chest, a gas-filled viscus or coiled nasogastric tube above the diaphragm, and lung compression. Herniation can be delayed for months or years. Because the diaphragm rises to about the fourth or fifth intercostal space in expiration, penetrating lower chest wounds can also injure it.

blocks.title: Chest trauma findings by mechanism
rows: Segment detached by double fractures of adjacent ribs
Hypoxemia worsening over 24 to 48 hours; nonlobar opacity
Air sucked through the wound; lung collapse
Blunt abdominal pressure surge or penetrating wound
Bowel or stomach in left hemithorax
blocks.caption: Each injury breaks one part of the rigid wall, sealed pleura, or airtight diaphragm.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with flail chest often become more hypoxemic the day after injury even though chest wall motion is unchanged?
blocks.explain: The underlying pulmonary contusion progresses as hemorrhage and edema fill more alveoli, increasing shunt over the first one to two days.
blocks.check: Compare with the description of pulmonary contusion in this section.

blocks.title: Two causes of shock after chest trauma
blocks.text: A driver hit the steering wheel and has hypotension, tachycardia, and absent breath sounds on the right. Absent breath sounds on one side mean air or fluid between lung and chest wall. Percussion separates them: hyperresonance means air, dullness means fluid. Neck veins then reveal the shock mechanism. Distended neck veins with the trachea pushed left indicate tension pneumothorax, where positive pleural pressure blocks venous return (obstructive shock). Flat neck veins with dullness indicate massive hemothorax, where volume is lost (hypovolemic shock). Cardiac tamponade also gives distended neck veins and hypotension, but breath sounds are present and heart sounds are muffled.

integration.text: Anatomy explains where these disorders arise and which side they affect. The thoracic duct crosses from right to left in the mid thorax, so the level of injury predicts the side of a chylothorax; intercostal and internal thoracic arteries carry systemic pressure, so they produce the dangerous hemothoraces; the liver shields the right hemidiaphragm; and the continuous mediastinal connective tissue lets air and infection spread from the alveoli or esophagus into the neck. Physiology unifies the bedside findings. Every condition either adds volume to the pleural space (fluid, blood, chyle, pus, air under tension), which pushes the mediastinum away, or removes volume from the lung (resorption or contraction atelectasis), which pulls it toward the lesion. Percussion then separates air from fluid, and neck veins separate obstructed venous return from lost volume.

Pathology and microbiology supply the fluid chemistry and the late outcomes. Starling forces decide transudate versus exudate; neutrophil and bacterial glycolysis explain the low glucose and pH of empyema; and organization of retained blood or pus by fibroblasts produces fibrothorax, the same repair process seen in any unresolved acute inflammation. Asbestos links occupational exposure to frustrated phagocytosis, fibrosis, and two cancers with different relationships to smoking. The limit of these rules is that bedside signs can be subtle in small collections or partial collapse, and that laboratory cutoffs such as Light criteria are probabilistic, so findings must be read together.

summary: The lung stays expanded because the sealed pleural space holds subatmospheric pressure between inward lung recoil and outward chest wall recoil.
Chylothorax is milky, lymphocyte-predominant fluid with triglycerides above 110 mg/dL and chylomicrons, from thoracic duct trauma, surgery, or lymphoma.
Hemothorax requires a pleural fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit; it causes hypovolemic shock early and fibrothorax from organized clot later.

Resorption atelectasis follows complete airway obstruction because venous blood has a subatmospheric total gas pressure; volume loss pulls the mediastinum toward the collapse, while compression by fluid or air pushes it away.
Calcified parietal pleural plaques are the most common asbestos lesion and mark exposure; asbestos multiplies smoking-related lung carcinoma risk, while mesothelioma risk is independent of smoking.
Pneumothorax gives hyperresonance with reduced or absent breath sounds; tension pneumothorax adds tracheal deviation away, hypotension, and distended neck veins from obstructed venous return.
An effusion is an exudate if any Light criterion is met: protein ratio above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit.
Heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome cause transudates; pneumonia, malignancy, tuberculosis, and pulmonary embolism cause exudates.
Empyema has low pH, low glucose, and high LDH; pneumomediastinum gives crepitus and the Hamman crunch; costochondritis pain is reproduced by palpation.
Flail segments move paradoxically, contusion hypoxemia worsens over 24 to 48 hours, sucking wounds collapse the lung, and blunt diaphragmatic rupture usually puts bowel in the left chest.

Asbestos risk figures (about fivefold alone and about 50 times with smoking for bronchogenic carcinoma) and mesothelioma latency vary between sources and are given as approximations.
Flail chest is defined as three or more adjacent ribs fractured in two or more places in most sources; some accept two ribs.
The two thirds of tracheal diameter rule for open pneumothorax and the 24 to 48 hour progression of pulmonary contusion are standard trauma teaching; confirm wording if tested.
Hemothorax capacity of each hemithorax (30% to 40% of blood volume) and the 200 mL threshold for blunting the costophrenic angle are approximate.
